name: chocolate
description: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which are toxic to dogs. Dark chocolate is more dangerous than milk chocolate.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/chocolate (accessed July 2025)

name: grapes
description: Grapes and raisins can cause acute kidney failure in dogs. The toxic substance is unknown.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/grapes (accessed July 2025)

name: xylitol
description: Xylitol causes rapid insulin release and severe hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) in dogs, leading to liver failure in high doses.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/xylitol (accessed July 2025)

name: macadamia nuts
description: Macadamia nuts cause weakness, depression, vomiting, tremors, and hyperthermia (elevated body temperature) in dogs.
action: Contact vet.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/macadamia-nuts (accessed July 2025)

name: coffee
description: Caffeine is toxic to dogs and can cause serious neurological symptoms and heart problems.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/coffee (accessed July 2025)

name: alcohol
description: Alcohol can cause severe intoxication, respiratory depression, coma, and death in dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/alcohol (accessed July 2025)

name: bread
description: Plain, cooked bread is safe for dogs in moderation. Avoid raw dough as it can expand and produce alcohol.
action: Offer in small amounts.

name: rice
description: Plain, cooked rice (white or brown) is easily digestible and often recommended for upset stomachs.
action: Offer in small amounts, plain.

name: pasta
description: Plain, cooked pasta is safe for dogs in moderation. Avoid sauces or seasonings.
action: Offer in small amounts, plain.

name: potato
description: Plain, cooked potatoes (without skin or green parts) are safe. Sweet potatoes are a good source of fiber.
action: Offer in small amounts, cooked and plain.

name: onions
description: All parts of onions and related plants are toxic to dogs, causing red blood cell damage (anemia).
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/onions-garlic (accessed July 2025)

name: avocado
description: Avocado contains 'persin,' which can cause vomiting and diarrhea in dogs. The pit is a choking hazard.
action: Monitor for symptoms; contact vet if severe.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/avocado (accessed July 2025)

name: cherries
description: Cherry pits, stems, and leaves contain cyanide, which is toxic. The fruit flesh is generally safe in small amounts, but pits are a choking hazard.
action: Contact vet if pits or large amounts ingested.

name: apple seeds
description: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide when digested. Small amounts are unlikely to cause harm, but large quantities can be dangerous.
action: Remove seeds before feeding apple flesh.

name: raw yeast dough
description: Raw yeast dough can expand in the stomach, causing bloating and potentially a life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV). Yeast also produces alcohol.
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: carrots
description: Carrots are a healthy, low-calorie snack. They can also help clean teeth.
action: Offer in moderation, cut into appropriate sizes.

name: apples
description: Apple flesh (without seeds or core) is a good source of vitamins and fiber. Always remove seeds and core.
action: Offer in moderation, remove seeds and core.

name: bananas
description: Bananas are a good source of potassium and vitamins. Offer in moderation due to sugar content.
action: Offer in moderation, peeled.

name: blueberries
description: Blueberries are packed with antioxidants and are a great low-calorie treat.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: green beans
description: Plain green beans (fresh or frozen, cooked) are a healthy, low-calorie snack, good for weight management.
action: Offer in moderation, plain.

name: cooked chicken
description: Plain, boneless, skinless, cooked chicken is an excellent source of protein and often used for upset stomachs.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: cooked salmon
description: Plain, cooked salmon (without bones or skin) is rich in Omega-3 fatty acids, beneficial for skin and coat.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: peanut butter
description: Xylitol-free peanut butter is a popular treat. Check labels carefully for xylitol.
action: Offer in moderation, check for xylitol.

name: pumpkin
description: Plain, cooked pumpkin (not pie filling) is excellent for digestive health due to its fiber content.
action: Offer in moderation, plain.

name: sweet potato
description: Plain, cooked sweet potato is a good source of dietary fiber, vitamins, and minerals.
action: Offer in moderation, cooked and plain.

name: eggs
description: Plain, cooked eggs are a great source of protein. Avoid raw eggs due to salmonella risk.
action: Offer in moderation, cooked and plain.

name: plain yogurt
description: Plain, unsweetened yogurt (without xylitol) can be a good source of probiotics for digestive health.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and unsweetened.

name: cheese
description: Small amounts of plain, low-fat cheese can be a treat. Too much can cause digestive upset due to lactose.
action: Offer in very small amounts, plain.

name: watermelon
description: Seedless watermelon (flesh only) is a hydrating, low-calorie treat. Remove all seeds and rind.
action: Offer in moderation, seedless and rind-free.

name: cucumber
description: Cucumbers are a healthy, low-calorie, hydrating snack.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: broccoli
description: Small amounts of cooked broccoli are safe and contain vitamins. Large amounts can cause digestive upset.
action: Offer in very small amounts, cooked.

name: spinach
description: Small amounts of cooked spinach are safe. High oxalate content means large amounts can interfere with calcium absorption.
action: Offer in very small amounts, cooked.

name: almonds
description: Almonds are not toxic but can cause stomach upset and are a choking hazard. High fat content can lead to pancreatitis.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: walnuts
description: Black walnuts are toxic, causing tremors and seizures. Other walnuts can cause digestive upset and pancreatitis due to high fat.
action: Contact vet if ingested, especially black walnuts.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/walnuts (accessed July 2025)

name: pecans
description: Pecans can cause stomach upset and pancreatitis due to high fat content. Moldy pecans may contain tremorgenic mycotoxins.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: wild mushrooms
description: Many wild mushrooms are highly toxic and can cause severe illness, organ failure, or death. Identification is difficult.
action: Contact vet immediately. Bring a sample of the mushroom if possible.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/mushrooms (accessed July 2025)

name: rhubarb
description: Rhubarb leaves contain oxalates, which can cause kidney problems. Stalks are less toxic but still not recommended.
action: Contact vet if leaves ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/rhubarb (accessed July 2025)

name: tomato plants
description: The green parts of tomato plants (leaves, stems, unripe fruit) contain solanine, which is toxic. Ripe red tomatoes are generally safe.
action: Contact vet if plant material ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/tomatoes (accessed July 2025)

name: lilies
description: True lilies (Lilium and Hemerocallis species) are highly toxic and can cause acute kidney failure in dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/lilies (accessed July 2025)

name: sago palm
description: All parts of the sago palm are highly toxic, especially the seeds, causing severe liver damage.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/sago-palm (accessed July 2025)

name: azalea
description: Azaleas and rhododendrons contain grayanotoxins, which can cause vomiting, diarrhea, cardiovascular issues, and central nervous system effects.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/azaleas-rhododendrons (accessed July 2025)

name: oleander
description: Oleander contains cardiac glycosides that are highly toxic to the heart, causing severe heart abnormalities and death.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/oleander (accessed July 2025)

name: daffodil
description: Daffodil bulbs are most toxic, containing lycorine, which causes vomiting and diarrhea. The flowers and stems are less toxic.
action: Contact vet if bulbs ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/daffodils (accessed July 2025)

name: tulip
description: Tulip bulbs contain allergenic lactones that can cause severe gastrointestinal upset.
action: Contact vet if bulbs ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/tulips (accessed July 2025)

name: poinsettia
description: Poinsettias are generally overrated in toxicity; they can cause mild irritation of the mouth and stomach upset.
action: Monitor, contact vet if symptoms persist.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/poinsettia (accessed July 2025)

name: aloe vera
description: The latex part of the aloe vera plant contains saponins and anthraquinones, which can cause digestive upset.
action: Contact vet if ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/aloe-vera (accessed July 2025)

name: ivy
description: Ivy plants contain triterpenoid saponins, which can cause gastrointestinal upset and dermatitis.
action: Contact vet if ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/ivy (accessed July 2025)

name: marijuana
description: THC in marijuana is toxic to dogs, causing central nervous system depression, ataxia, and sometimes seizures or coma.
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: NSAIDs
description: Human NSAIDs can cause severe stomach ulcers, kidney failure, and liver damage in dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/human-medications (accessed July 2025)

name: acetaminophen
description: Acetaminophen is highly toxic to dogs, causing liver damage and red blood cell damage (methemoglobinemia).
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/human-medications (accessed July 2025)

name: antidepressants
description: Human antidepressants can cause neurological symptoms like sedation, agitation, tremors, and seizures in dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/human-medications (accessed July 2025)

name: cold medicines
description: Many cold medicines contain ingredients like pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine (stimulants) or acetaminophen, all highly toxic to dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/human-medications (accessed July 2025)

name: iron supplements
description: Iron overdose can cause severe gastrointestinal upset, liver damage, and heart problems.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/human-medications (accessed July 2025)

name: cleaning products
description: Corrosive or irritating chemicals can cause severe burns to the mouth, esophagus, and stomach, or systemic toxicity.
action: Contact vet immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/cleaning-products (accessed July 2025)

name: antifreeze
description: Ethylene glycol is highly toxic, causing acute kidney failure. Even a small amount can be fatal.
action: Contact vet immediately. Time is critical.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/antifreeze (accessed July 2025)

name: rodenticides
description: Rodenticides come in various types (anticoagulants, bromethalin, cholecalciferol) each causing severe, often delayed, and fatal effects.
action: Contact vet immediately. Bring packaging if possible.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/rodenticides (accessed July 2025)

name: insecticides
description: Insecticides can cause a range of symptoms from mild digestive upset to severe neurological effects depending on the chemical.
action: Contact vet immediately. Bring packaging if possible.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/insecticides (accessed July 2025)

name: batteries
description: Batteries can cause corrosive burns to the mouth, esophagus, and stomach due to their alkaline contents. Lithium button batteries are especially dangerous.
action: Contact vet immediately. Do NOT induce vomiting.

name: essential oils
description: Many essential oils are toxic when ingested or applied to skin, causing liver damage, neurological issues, or skin irritation.
action: Contact vet.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/essential-oils (accessed July 2025)

name: dryer sheets
description: Dryer sheets contain cationic detergents that can cause mouth ulcers, vomiting, and internal irritation.
action: Contact vet if ingested.

name: cooked bones
description: Cooked bones become brittle and can splinter, causing choking, internal punctures, or blockages.
action: Contact vet immediately if ingested.

name: raw meat
description: Raw meat can contain harmful bacteria (Salmonella, E. coli) and parasites, posing risks to both dogs and humans.
action: Avoid feeding raw meat.

name: raw fish
description: Raw fish can contain thiaminase (an enzyme that destroys thiamine/Vitamin B1) and parasites, especially salmon from the Pacific Northwest.
action: Avoid feeding raw fish.

name: fatty foods
description: High-fat foods can cause pancreatitis (inflammation of the pancreas), which is a serious and painful condition.
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: salt
description: Excessive salt intake can lead to sodium ion poisoning, causing neurological symptoms and dehydration.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/salt (accessed July 2025)

name: corn on the cob
description: While corn kernels are safe, the cob itself is indigestible and can cause a severe intestinal blockage.
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: nutmeg
description: Nutmeg contains myristicin, which can cause hallucinations, disorientation, and central nervous system effects in large doses.
action: Contact vet if large amount ingested.

name: yeast
description: Raw yeast can ferment in the stomach, producing alcohol and causing bloating (similar to raw dough).
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: raw eggs
description: Raw eggs can contain Salmonella bacteria, and raw egg whites contain avidin, which can interfere with biotin absorption over time.
action: Avoid feeding raw eggs.

name: milk
description: Many dogs are lactose intolerant and milk can cause digestive upset. Small amounts are generally not harmful.
action: Offer in very small amounts, or avoid if sensitive.

name: ice cream
description: Ice cream contains dairy (lactose), sugar, and sometimes xylitol or chocolate, all potentially harmful.
action: Avoid or offer dog-specific frozen treats.

name: citrus fruits
description: Citrus stems, leaves, peels, and seeds contain citric acid and essential oils which can cause digestive upset. The fruit flesh is generally safe in small amounts.
action: Avoid peels, stems, leaves; small amounts of flesh are usually fine.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/citrus (accessed July 2025)

name: peaches
description: Peach pits contain cyanide and are a choking hazard. The flesh is safe in moderation.
action: Remove pit before feeding flesh.

name: plums
description: Plum pits contain cyanide and are a choking hazard. The flesh is safe in moderation.
action: Remove pit before feeding flesh.

name: apricots
description: Apricot pits contain cyanide and are a choking hazard. The flesh is safe in moderation.
action: Remove pit before feeding flesh.

name: cooked corn
description: Plain, cooked corn kernels are safe and digestible. Avoid corn on the cob.
action: Offer in moderation, off the cob.

name: strawberries
description: Strawberries are safe and contain antioxidants. Offer in moderation due to sugar content.
action: Offer in moderation, washed.

name: raspberries
description: Raspberries are safe and contain antioxidants. Offer in moderation due to naturally occurring xylitol in very small amounts.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: blackberries
description: Blackberries are safe and contain antioxidants and fiber. Offer in moderation.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: pears
description: Pear flesh (without seeds or core) is safe and a good source of fiber. Remove seeds and core.
action: Offer in moderation, remove seeds and core.

name: lettuce
description: Lettuce is safe and hydrating, but offers little nutritional value. Can cause mild digestive upset in large amounts.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: celery
description: Celery is a safe, low-calorie snack. Cut into small pieces to prevent choking.
action: Offer in moderation, cut small.

name: bell peppers
description: Bell peppers are safe and a good source of vitamins. Avoid spicy peppers.
action: Offer in moderation, avoid seeds and stem.

name: cabbage
description: Small amounts of cooked cabbage are safe. Large amounts can cause gas.
action: Offer in very small amounts, cooked.

name: brussels sprouts
description: Small amounts of cooked brussels sprouts are safe. Large amounts can cause gas.
action: Offer in very small amounts, cooked.

name: peanuts
description: Plain, unsalted peanuts are safe in moderation. High fat content means too many can cause digestive upset.
action: Offer in moderation, unsalted.

name: cashews
description: Plain, unsalted cashews are safe in moderation. High fat content can cause digestive upset.
action: Offer in moderation, unsalted.

name: plain popcorn
description: Plain, air-popped popcorn (without butter, salt, or toppings) is safe in moderation. Unpopped kernels are a choking hazard.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and air-popped.

name: oatmeal
description: Plain, cooked oatmeal (without sugar or flavorings) is a good source of fiber and can help with digestive issues.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: quinoa
description: Plain, cooked quinoa is a safe and nutritious grain for dogs in moderation.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: turkey
description: Plain, boneless, skinless, cooked turkey is a good source of protein. Avoid fatty skin or seasoned meat.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: pork
description: Plain, cooked pork (without excessive fat or seasoning) is safe in moderation. Avoid raw or undercooked pork.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: green peas
description: Green peas (fresh or frozen, cooked) are a healthy source of vitamins and fiber.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: canned tuna
description: Plain, canned tuna in water (not oil) is safe in small amounts. High mercury content means it should be an occasional treat.
action: Offer in very small amounts, in water.

name: water chestnuts
description: Water chestnuts are safe for dogs and can be a crunchy treat. Offer in moderation.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: peppers (spicy)
description: Spicy peppers contain capsaicin, which causes irritation and digestive upset.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: raw potatoes
description: Raw potatoes, especially green parts and sprouts, contain solanine, which is toxic. Cooked potatoes are safe.
action: Avoid feeding raw potatoes.

name: cinnamon
description: Cinnamon is not highly toxic in small amounts, but large quantities can cause mouth irritation, digestive upset, or respiratory issues if inhaled.
action: Avoid feeding large amounts.

name: nutella
description: Nutella contains chocolate (cocoa), sugar, and fat, all of which can be harmful to dogs. While cocoa content is low, large amounts are risky.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: garlic bread
description: Garlic is toxic to dogs and can cause red blood cell damage. Even small amounts in garlic bread can be harmful.
action: Contact vet if ingested.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/onions-garlic (accessed July 2025)

name: grapes (dried)
description: Dried grapes (raisins, currants) are just as toxic as fresh grapes and can cause acute kidney failure.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/grapes (accessed July 2025)

name: chives
description: Chives, like other members of the Allium family (onions, garlic), are toxic and can cause red blood cell damage.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/onions-garlic (accessed July 2025)

name: licorice
description: Licorice can cause vomiting and diarrhea. In large amounts, it can affect blood pressure and electrolyte balance.
action: Contact vet if large amount ingested.

name: hops
description: Hops, used in brewing beer, can cause malignant hyperthermia (rapid, dangerous increase in body temperature) in dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/hops (accessed July 2025)

name: milk chocolate
description: While less toxic than dark chocolate, milk chocolate still contains theobromine and caffeine, which are harmful to dogs.
action: Contact vet, especially if large amount.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/chocolate (accessed July 2025)

name: dark chocolate
description: Dark chocolate contains high levels of theobromine and caffeine, making it very dangerous for dogs.
action: Contact vet immediately.
citations: ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center: https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/chocolate (accessed July 2025)

name: raw salmon
description: Raw Pacific salmon can carry a parasite that causes 'Salmon Poisoning Disease,' which is fatal if untreated.
action: Contact vet immediately.

name: raw eggs (whites)
description: Raw egg whites contain avidin, which can inhibit biotin absorption, leading to skin and coat problems over time.
action: Avoid feeding raw egg whites regularly.

name: cooked beef
description: Plain, lean, cooked beef (without seasonings or excessive fat) is a good source of protein.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: cooked lamb
description: Plain, cooked lamb (without excessive fat or seasoning) is safe and often well-tolerated.
action: Offer in moderation, plain and cooked.

name: white bread
description: Plain white bread in small amounts is generally safe, but offers little nutritional value. Avoid raw dough.
action: Offer in small amounts.

name: popcorn (buttered/salted)
description: Buttered and salted popcorn can lead to digestive upset, dehydration, and potentially sodium ion poisoning.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: cooked shrimp
description: Plain, cooked shrimp (shelled and deveined) is safe in moderation and a good source of protein. Avoid raw shrimp.
action: Offer in moderation, cooked and plain.

name: cooked carrots
description: Cooked carrots are easily digestible and a healthy, low-calorie treat.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: cooked peas
description: Cooked peas are a good source of vitamins, minerals, and fiber.
action: Offer in moderation.

name: cooked broccoli florets
description: Small amounts of cooked broccoli florets are safe and provide vitamins. Large amounts can cause gas.
action: Offer in very small amounts, cooked.

name: raw sweet potato
description: Raw sweet potatoes can be difficult to digest and may cause intestinal upset or blockage.
action: Always cook sweet potatoes before feeding.

name: corn syrup
description: While not directly toxic, corn syrup is pure sugar and can lead to obesity, dental problems, and diabetes with regular consumption.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: cat food
description: Cat food is formulated for cats' nutritional needs (higher protein, different vitamin balance) and is not suitable as a regular diet for dogs, potentially leading to nutritional deficiencies or obesity over time.
action: Avoid feeding regularly; occasional small amounts are generally not harmful.

name: macaroni and cheese
description: Macaroni and cheese is high in fat, dairy, and often salt, which can cause digestive upset and pancreatitis in dogs.
action: Avoid feeding.

name: persimmons
description: Fruit flesh may be tolerated in small amounts, but the seeds and skin can cause intestinal upset or blockage.
action: Avoid seeds and skin; contact vet if signs of blockage occur.

name: pomegranate arils
description: Small amounts of arils are generally safe but can upset sensitive stomachs.
action: Offer only a few arils; avoid rind and large quantities.

name: star fruit
description: Contains oxalates which can affect kidneys; not recommended for dogs.
action: Avoid feeding; contact vet if ingested.

name: dragon fruit
description: Mild, hydrating fruit; seeds are soft and typically pass without issue.
action: Offer in small amounts; remove thick peel.

name: guava (ripe flesh)
description: Tropical fruit safe in moderation; firm seeds can be irritating.
action: Offer small pieces; avoid hard seeds and rind.

name: lychee (without seed)
description: Sweet fruit; the large seed is a choking hazard and should be removed.
action: Peel and fully remove seed; offer sparingly due to sugar.

name: dates (without pits)
description: Energy-dense fruit; high sugar may cause GI upset if overfed.
action: Use rarely as a tiny treat; ensure pits are removed.

name: figs (fresh)
description: Fiber-rich fruit; may cause loose stool in sensitive dogs.
action: Offer in small amounts; avoid leaves/plant which can irritate.

name: cranberries
description: Tart berries; avoid sweetened or trail mixes with raisins.
action: Offer sparingly; avoid products mixed with raisins or xylitol.

name: coconut (flesh)
description: Fatty treat that can cause GI upset in excess; avoid sweetened coconut.
action: Offer a small amount only; avoid sweeteners and large flakes.

name: coconut water (unsweetened)
description: Electrolyte-containing drink; small amounts are typically fine.
action: Offer a few sips only; avoid added sugar and flavors.

name: bone broth (plain)
description: Hydrating, palatable liquid; must be onion/garlic-free and low sodium.
action: Use plain, unsalted, allium-free; cool and skim fat.

name: nori (seaweed sheets)
description: Unsalted, plain nori can be a low-calorie snack.
action: Offer tiny pieces; avoid seasoned or salted varieties.

name: chickpeas (cooked)
description: Cooked, plain legumes offering fiber and protein.
action: Rinse and serve plain in small amounts; avoid hummus (seasonings).

name: lentils (cooked)
description: Cooked and plain, lentils are generally well tolerated.
action: Serve plain and soft; small portions only.

name: black beans (cooked)
description: Cooked plain beans are safe; canned beans should be rinsed to reduce sodium.
action: Offer small amounts; avoid added salt, onion, or spices.

name: barley (cooked)
description: Cooked grain that’s gentle on some stomachs.
action: Serve plain and fully cooked in small portions.

name: couscous (plain)
description: Small-grain pasta that’s safe when plain and fully cooked.
action: Offer a spoonful or two; no butter, salt, or spices.

name: bulgur (cooked)
description: Whole grain option; provide fiber when served plain.
action: Cook thoroughly and serve plain in small amounts.

name: polenta (plain)
description: Plain, cooked cornmeal can be an occasional carb source.
action: Serve a small amount; avoid butter, cheese, or seasoning.

name: chia seeds (soaked)
description: Soaked chia can add fiber and omega-3s; dry seeds can swell.
action: Pre-soak; offer a pinch mixed into food.

name: ground flaxseed
description: Source of fiber and ALA omega-3s.
action: Offer a small sprinkle on meals; avoid whole seeds for best digestion.

name: pumpkin seeds (plain, roasted)
description: Plain roasted seeds (unsalted) may be offered sparingly.
action: Offer only a few; avoid salt, oil, or seasoning.

name: basil
description: Culinary herb that’s safe in tiny amounts.
action: Use as a garnish-sized treat only; avoid oils/extracts.

name: parsley
description: Herb safe in very small amounts; large quantities are not advised.
action: Use a pinch; avoid essential oils and large doses.

name: cilantro
description: Leafy herb that can add aroma without salt or fat.
action: Offer a few chopped leaves as garnish only.

name: dill
description: Aromatic herb; safe in tiny amounts.
action: Use sparingly; avoid pickled products (salt).

name: rosemary
description: Fragrant herb; tiny amounts are generally fine.
action: Offer a pinch; avoid concentrated extracts.

name: mint (culinary)
description: Culinary mints are typically safe in tiny amounts; note that pennyroyal mint is toxic.
action: Offer a leaf or two; avoid essential oils and pennyroyal species.

name: oregano (fresh)
description: Fresh leaves in tiny amounts are usually tolerated; essential oil is not.
action: Use a pinch; do not use oregano oil on or in dogs.

name: philodendron
